key_insight: A focused empirical comparison shows which design choices in vision–language–action (VLA) models actually drive useful, generalist robotic behavior — not just bigger models, but better multimodal alignment, action grounding, and task-tailored data.
problem_solved: Clarifies which components and engineering decisions make VLA models effective for controlling diverse robots, addressing confusion about where to invest effort (model scale, pretraining, fine‑tuning, or data collection) when building generalist robot agents.
method: Systematic empirical comparison of representative VLA model designs across shared benchmarks and tasks
Controlled ablation studies isolating factors such as vision encoder, language backbone, action decoder, pretraining corpus, and fine‑tuning strategy
Evaluation on a mix of simulated and real-world manipulation/navigation tasks to measure generalization and practical usefulness
impact: Provides actionable guidance for researchers and engineers on which architectural and data choices yield the biggest gains for embodied, language-guided robots — enabling more efficient development of robust generalist agents without blindly scaling every component.
visual_elements: Architecture comparison diagram showing vision encoder → language module → action decoder variants
Bar/heatmap of ablation results highlighting the relative importance of data, alignment, and fine‑tuning
Pipeline infographic illustrating pretraining → alignment/fine‑tuning → deployment on real robot
Task gallery (icons) showing benchmark tasks used for evaluation: manipulation, navigation, multi‑step instructions
paper_title: What matters in building vision–language–action models for generalist robots
paper_authors: Xinghang Li, Peiyan Li, Long Qian, Minghuan Liu, Dong Wang
